The random chunk of iron is because speaker cones are almost always made of paper basically and paper is non magnetic and magets are used to move the paper cone. Via a chunk of metal attached. text: Don Ziolkowski Attached to the back of the cone is a copper (or sometime aluminium) coil. It sits in a gap between the top plate and pole piece of the magnet. The top and bottom plate are iron, but they are part of the magnet (of which the magnetic material is ferrite or neodymium) not attached to the cone. You want the cone to be as light as possible while still being strong, so you definitely do not want to attach a lump of iron to it. The diagram shown makes absolutely no sense. jonnathan deven I never said you couldnt do that, its just not supposed to be that way. The problem with putting subwoofers in an enclosure with other speakers is that the air volume displaced by the subwoofer cone excursion pushes the cone of any other speakers within the enclosure. Unless the other speakers in the enclosure are the same type/size of speaker, the subwoofer will be dampened by the other speakers, or you could possibly rip the cone out of the other speakers if they are significantly smaller than the subwoofer.

The main point is, you will never find a subfwooer in a speaker like the one used in the image.

Tweeters take care of the higher frequency’s, woofers handle the mid-low frequency’s, and a subwoofer handles the really low frequency’s. author: @heyitsme939

text:
@heyitsme The most common audio setup in a 3 way speaker as they pictured would not exclude a midrange speaker and include a subwoofer. tweeters handle high frequency(>2000hz), mid-range as the name implies handles mid frequency(~250-2000hz), woofer handles low frequency(up to max ~500hz).
Sub-woofer handles very low frequency(from 20hz to maximum of ~200hz), almost always in a seperate unit, and probably more commonly used for movies than music in a home. Subwoofers only became common in the 90s.
Using tweeter + woofer + subwoofer would miss the middle range completely.
Sometimes 1 driver would handle woofer & mid-range frquencies, but I think that would usually only be with 2-way speakers(speaker units that only have tweeter + 1 other driver, perhaps the tweet would go lower than usual too) I guess the woofer/mid-range driver may be little if at all different physically, but have a different crossover setup.

text:
There are way more kinds of speaker components though.. 
But the common types of speaker drivers are as following:

Tweeter - High frequency driver typically assigned to produce sound waves above 2 kHz
* Dome Tweeters, Horn-loaded tweeters, Piezo-electric tweeters are some of the more common types of high frequency drivers.

Mid-range drivers - Name is as it sounds (litarally), these are drivers that's assigned to the vocal spectrum of sound, typically between 200-2000 Hz
* Mid-range drivers are commonly sized between 3-6.5" (7.5-17 cm)

Woofer - Low frequency drivers commonly assigned to play the low-end of the sonic spectrum, usually from 200 Hz and down. 
However, there are in certain circumstances drivers that is used as both woofers and mid-ranges at the same time. These are referred to as mid-bass drivers
Another variant of the mid-woofer used in car applications is specifically assigned to play kick-bass and frequencies above 50 Hz. 

Subwoofer - Large very low frequency drivers assigned to play the bass sections below 80-100 Hz
There is also a wide variety of subwoofers available, such as: 
Competition-grade (SPL) - These are normally the big beefy ones commonly used in car-audio applications
Sound Quality drivers - The high-end home-theater subwoofers fall into this category
Professional - The kind of subwoofers used in concerts and at big events
Everyday listening-grade - Cheaper and smaller alternatives of the aforementioned usually fall into this category

text: I agree that the subwoofers usually have their own enclosures, and should, because it can cause frequency distortion and overall bad sound. I also believe it is correct that the "subwoofer" in the three speaker enclosure is not actually a "subwoofer", but probably something similar. The speaker classifications kind of differ between who you're talking to. Some people say that there are only two, bass and treble, some say that there are 3, bass, midrange and high, and others, like myself like to classify them as I would set them up in most music listening environments, bass, mid-bass, midrange and high. It's not so much as it has to have that many classifications, it's just that when you set up a performance audio system you tend to have four different driver types so as to create a more stable SPL (sound pressure level) on all frequencies and higher volume without clipping or sound distortion.

text:
It's best to have as few types of drivers as possible. It's easily audible when a sound of a bridge frequency (ex. 2000Hz, that can either be rendered by the mid-range speaker or by the tweeter) is played by one driver or another.
So, judging that the human ear can hear from 40Hz to 20000Hz, and the body can feel from about 20-30Hz, it is reasonable to suggest that having speakers that render the 30-20k range with ~100db fidelity.
In this case, a woofer that renders 30-2000Hz + a tweeter is a very good way to go.

Subwoofers are often overkill, and spoil the quality of the music, if you already have a speaker system capable of offering as low as 30Hz at high fidelity.

text:
Your sound card may have both digital and analog outputs. The 3.5mm jack, for instance, is analog. An SPDIF output, usually an optical signal, is digital.
Either way, some device must convert the signal to analog before it hits your speaker. This is called a DAC; and that analog signal must be of sufficient amplitude to drive your speaker; this is achieved by an amplifier.
You don't typically but just a DAC or just an amplifier; most sound cards, and almost all home theater receivers have both inside.
Your speakers convert an analog electrical signal to a mechanical signal (sound).

Ok here goes i have to take issue with your explanation of drive units, in my opinion i think you have made a bit of an error let me explain why i think you have made an error. "Tweeters" ok desighned to produce high frequency sounds " a bird tweet tweet " 2. Next drive unit  down the chain is the "Mid Range" unit and as its name say's it is designed to handle most of the mid range frequencies 3. The third unit being the "Bass unit" which by definition is designed to handle the lower frequencies. These three drive units have been the basic combination of drive units configured with in a cabinet to form what we call "Speakers".  While you dont have to use all three drive units in order to make a pair of speakers there are also two way systems and fourway systems by the use of a driver above a tweeter called a "super high frequency driver" or an "ABR" Auxilliary Bass Radiator. The use of an extra low frequency drive unit or "Sub" has only become popular over recent years , the so called "Subs" that are now so popular are a newish desire.

Most people will be very happy to enjoy and use the traditional pair of speakers as we know them without the need for the "Sub" speaker, this is not a definative explanation of the most used drive units how ever i think it gives better clarity, let's not also forget the likes of Tannoy who are world leaders in using  what looks like a single drive unit but is actually two units in one with the high frequency unit situated down the center at the rear in a compression driver format. lets not forget that all the drive units in the world are no good if a suitable cross over network is not used in order to seperate out all the different frequencies and send them to the correct drive units.

text:
The strategically placed holes thing is WRONG.
Look it up: bass reflex port. That's the technical term and the function it serves is to enlarge the frequency range of the woofer by creating a tube with a lower ground resonance then the speaker itself has.
This is my understanding and it's probably not 100% accurate, but bass reflex ports are NOT for supplying air.

You'd rather have an airtight speaker than one with a "regular" hole in it, because the enclosement will work better that way. The hole is actually more like a tunnel with a very specific length and diameter designed for the enclosure and speaker to have these results. This involves complicated physics for designing and I would discourage people building their own speakers to cut holes in their enclosure.

I understand this video was made to be as fast as possible and that things need to be oversimplified to keep it short, but this was just wrong information.

It's not that hard to do a bit of research and this is basic speaker knowledge.
